blocks.text: Every Russian noun is **masculine**, **feminine** or **neuter**, and you can almost always tell which from the last letter of the dictionary form:

head: Gender
Ends in…
Examples
rows: m. слова́рь, день · f. дверь, ночь

blocks.text: Words ending in **-ь** must be learned one by one, though nouns in **-ость** (ра́дость, *joy*) and **-сть**, **-чь**, **-шь**, **-щь** are feminine.

Words for men are masculine even when they end in **-а** or **-я**: **па́па**, **дя́дя** (*uncle*), **мужчи́на** (*man*), and the short names **Са́ша**, **Ва́ня**. Adjectives agree with the man: *мой* папа, *хороший* мужчина.
Why it matters: adjectives, *my* and *this*, and past-tense verbs all change to match a noun's gender — **мой** брат, **моя** сестра; он чит**ал**, она чит**ала**.

exercises.why: A man, so masculine — though it ends in -а.

exercises.q: Which is the odd one out?
exercises.why: **Мама** is feminine; the others end in -о/-е and are neuter.
An uncle is a man: **мой**, despite the -я.
